title: Collective self-sorting on a chip
authors: Emanuel F. Teixeira, Thieu van den Bergh, Arjen Klok, Tijn Heesakkers, Alexandre Morin
abstract: We harness two established ingredients for collective demixing: differential speed and curvature to create a self-sorting device. In binary mixtures, motility differences drive spontaneous spatial segregation, while confinement geometry determines how rapidly and strongly this demixing develops. Using particle based simulations, we systematically identify the geometrical conditions that promote efficient segregation and use these results to guide the design of a finite sorting architecture. We then translate these physical mechanisms into a sequence of curved microfluidic units that progressively amplify the separation of the two species and direct them toward distinct collection regions. Experiments with binary Quincke-roller mixtures confirm that an initially mixed suspension progressively demixes as it propagates through the device, leading to strong enrichment downstream. Our results demonstrate how collective active demixing can be converted into a functional continuous sorting strategy, providing a route toward autonomous microfluidic separation based on particle motility and confinement geometry.
summary: This work demonstrates how the inherent tendency of active particles to demix due to differences in self-propulsion speed can be engineered into a functional, continuous sorting device. By controlling the geometry of curved microfluidic channels, the authors successfully convert a microscopic active demixing process into a macroscopic, high-purity separation technique. This provides a powerful blueprint for autonomous microfluidic separation based on particle motility.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a functional, continuous sorting strategy by harnessing collective active demixing in binary mixtures of self-propelled particles.
main_result: By designing a sequence of curved microfluidic units, the initial mixed suspension progressively demixes, leading to strong, controllable enrichment of the two species at distinct collection regions.
method: The study combines particle-based molecular dynamics simulations with experimental measurements using Quincke-roller mixtures in microfluidic channels.
model_or_system: The system involves binary mixtures of active particles exhibiting differential self-propulsion speed and excluded-volume interactions, confined within geometries ranging from circular wells to complex, snake-like annular channels.
key_observables: Spatial segregation patterns, demixing parameter ($\gamma$), normalized throughput ($	ilde{Q}_k$), and particle density fractions ($\chi_k$) at various downstream locations.
important_parameters: Differential self-propulsion speed, confinement geometry (e.g., $R_{in}/R_{out}$ ratio, wall position $w$), and the number of sequential sorting units ($N_{units}$).
main_assumptions: The demixing mechanism is robust and can be controlled by geometry; the simulation models excluded-volume interactions and particle dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate radial demixing in circular wells (Fig. 1a), the acceleration of demixing in smaller confinements (Fig. 2), the control of segregation by boundary geometry (Fig. 3), and the final realization in a snake-like channel showing progressive enrichment (Fig. 6).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the fundamental mechanism of demixing using simple circular wells, to optimizing the geometry using annular channels and periodic boundary conditions, and finally demonstrating the scalability by constructing and testing a finite, continuous 'snake-like' sorting device.
why_interesting: While the core physics is classical active matter, the principles of non-equilibrium phase separation, pattern formation, and directed transport in confined geometries are highly relevant to understanding energy dissipation and collective dynamics in quantum many-body systems or engineered quantum devices.
